title: 1:1 vs 1:2
hook: Win rate is not the whole edge.

launchpad.outcome: Compare risk-to-reward structures and read a simple expectancy, without turning it into a promise.
launchpad.missionQuestion: Does a strategy need to win most trades?

slides.title: Move the sliders

asks.prompt: DOES A STRATEGY NEED TO WIN MOST OF ITS TRADES TO HAVE POSITIVE EXPECTANCY?

options.label: Yes
options.feedback: 40% wins at +2R vs −1R is +0.20R per trade, in theory.

options.label: No
options.why: Win rate and payoff work together.

asks.prompt: DOES USING 1:2 AUTOMATICALLY GIVE A STRATEGY POSITIVE EXPECTANCY?

options.label: Yes
options.feedback: Only if the win rate, average win and average loss actually support it.

options.label: No
options.why: You need real win rate, average win and loss, consistent execution, costs and a big enough sample.

slides.punch: WIN RATE IS NOT THE WHOLE EDGE.

slides.quote: 1:2 isn’t an edge by itself. It’s a structure. The edge is in what actually happens over a real sample.

slides.prompt: Why isn’t win rate the whole story?
slides.modelAnswer: Because expectancy depends on how much I win when I win and lose when I lose. A 40% win rate can be positive at 1:2, and a 1:2 structure can still be negative if the real win rate, costs or execution don’t support it.

takeaways: Theory, before costs, over a real sample.
remember: Win rate is not the whole edge.
